meta.title: Who really said "A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write, if he is to be ultimately at peace with himself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Maslow wrote it — in Motivation and Personality (1954). His 1943 Psychological Review original ends "ultimately happy," not "at peace with himself."

answer.sourceLine: This is real Maslow, word for word — it opens the section headed “The Need for Self-Actualization” in Motivation and Personality, first published in 1954 and read here in the second edition (Harper & Row, 1970) at p. 46. One wrinkle worth knowing: the sentence began life in his 1943 Psychological Review paper, where it ends “if he is to be ultimately happy” — the familiar “at peace with himself” is Maslow’s own later revision for the book.

source.excerpt: A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write, if he is to be ultimately at peace with himself. What a man can be, he must be. He must be true to his own nature. This need we may call self-actualization.
trail: 1943 — the first draft of the thought. In “A Theory of Human Motivation,” Psychological Review 50, no. 4, Maslow writes at p. 382: “A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write, if he is to be ultimately happy.” The full text is hosted by York University’s Classics in the History of Psychology ↗.

1954 — the wording everyone now quotes. The paper is reworked into Motivation and Personality, where the sentence ends “if he is to be ultimately at peace with himself” and gains the follow-on “He must be true to his own nature.” The passage sits at p. 46 of the second edition, Harper & Row, New York, 1970 ↗.

Today — the line travels without its book. Wikiquote ↗ records the “at peace with himself” wording twice: once under Motivation and Personality (1954), p. 93, and once — less accurately — under the 1943 article.
The companion sentence gets its own life. “What a man can be, he must be” is quoted on its own constantly; Wikipedia’s hierarchy-of-needs article ↗ cites it to Maslow 1954, p. 91.
source.excerptNote: Immediately before this, Maslow observes that even when every other need is satisfied a new restlessness sets in unless a person is doing what he is individually fitted for. The sentence is the hinge of the whole concept — it is where self-actualization enters the hierarchy.

author.name: Abraham Maslow
author.kicker: The man who put self-actualization at the top
author.heading: Who was Abraham Maslow?
author.metaLine: 1908–1970 · American psychologist · founder of humanistic psychology
author.bio: Abraham Harold Maslow (1 April 1908 – 8 June 1970) was an American psychologist who taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis and is remembered above all for the hierarchy of needs he first laid out in a 1943 Psychological Review paper. Where the psychology of his day studied illness, Maslow insisted on studying flourishing — what people are like when nothing is broken. He expanded that paper into Motivation and Personality (1954), the book that carries this sentence and that made “self-actualization” — a term he credits in the same passage to Kurt Goldstein — part of everyday language.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong source
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fabrication — Maslow really wrote it. What goes wrong is the citation: the line is routinely pinned to his famous 1943 paper, which contains a different last clause.

items.why: The 1943 article’s own text reads “A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write, if he is to be ultimately happy” — see the page-382 marker in the full text at Classics in the History of Psychology ↗. The familiar “at peace with himself” belongs to the book, not the paper; even Wikiquote ↗ lists the “at peace” wording under the 1943 citation.

The book ran to three editions and the pagination moved. Wikiquote ↗ gives p. 93 for the 1954 edition, while Wikipedia ↗ cites Maslow 1954, p. 91 for the next sentence; in the 1970 second edition ↗ the passage sits at p. 46. A page number without an edition is not really a citation.

items.who: “What one can be, one must be”
items.why: The gender-neutral rewrite circulates widely on quote graphics, but Maslow’s text — in both the 1943 paper and the book — reads “What a man can be, he must be,” with the emphasis falling on the two verbs. That is an observation from the printed pages themselves, not a claim about who first reworded it.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Maslow — but quote it from Motivation and Personality (1954), not from the 1943 paper ↗, where the sentence ends “ultimately happy.”

context.heading: Why the changed word matters
lead: Maslow spent 1943 arguing that human needs stack: satisfy hunger and safety turns up; satisfy safety and belonging turns up. The sentence about the musician, the artist and the poet is where the stack runs out of ordinary answers — the point at which someone with everything is still restless, because he is not doing the thing he is built to do.

When he rebuilt the paper into Motivation and Personality, Maslow quietly swapped “ultimately happy” for “ultimately at peace with himself,” and added a line: “He must be true to his own nature.” It is a small edit that changes the promise. Self-actualization stops being a route to happiness and becomes something closer to a debt you owe your own capacities — which is, not coincidentally, the version that stuck.
detailsBody: Maslow is explicit in the same passage that he did not coin the word: he credits Kurt Goldstein, and says he is using it in a “more specific and limited fashion” than Goldstein did. The familiar pyramid diagram came later still — Maslow himself drew no pyramid in this chapter.
